arXiv:2505.01513v2 [cond-mat.quant-gas] 15 Dec 2025

Engineering frustrated Rydberg spin models by graphical Floquet modulation

Mingsheng Tian Affiliation: Department of Physics, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania, 16802, USA    Rhine Samajdar Email: rhine_samajdar@princeton.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA Affiliation: Princeton Center for Theoretical Science, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA    Bryce Gadway Email: bgadway@psu.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania, 16802, USA
Abstract

Arrays of Rydberg atoms interacting via dipole-dipole interactions offer a powerful platform for probing quantum many-body physics. However, these intrinsic interactions also determine and constrain the models—and parameter regimes thereof—for quantum simulation. Here, we propose a systematic framework to engineer arbitrary desired long-range interactions in Rydberg-atom lattices, enabling the realization of fully tunable J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} Heisenberg models. Using site-resolved periodic modulation of Rydberg states, we develop an experimentally feasible protocol to precisely control the interaction ratios J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} and J3/J1J_{3}/J_{1} in a kagome lattice. This control can increase the effective range of interactions and drive transitions between competing spin-ordered and spin liquid phases. To generalize this approach beyond the kagome lattice, we reformulate the design of modulation patterns through a graph-theoretic approach, demonstrating the universality of our method across all 11 planar Archimedean lattices. Our strategy overcomes the inherent constraints of power-law-decaying dipolar interactions, providing a versatile toolbox for exploring frustrated magnetism, emergent topological phases, and quantum correlations in systems with long-range interactions.

Introduction.—In recent years, a variety of programmable quantum simulators have emerged as powerful tools for probing the physics of strongly interacting quantum systems [1, 2]. Rydberg atom arrays offer one such promising platform due to their combination of tunable geometries and strong, controllable interactions [3]. Rapid advances in experimental techniques have allowed for the precise trapping and manipulation of neutral atoms in arrays, enabling the exploration of a wide range of many-body phenomena, ranging from correlated quantum phases [4, 5, 6] to nonequilibrium quantum dynamics [7, 8, 9, 10]. A landmark achievement in this regard was the preparation of a topological ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} quantum spin liquid (QSL) state [11, 12, 13], a highly entangled phase of matter which had been sought after in solid-state materials for nearly half a century [14, 15].

Despite this remarkable progress, an apparent limitation of Rydberg simulators lies in the precise nature of the interactions, which typically decay as a power law with distance. This decay restricts the ability to fully investigate models requiring flexible and tunable long-range interactions [16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. When appropriately chosen, such interactions can introduce geometric frustration and enhance quantum fluctuations, leading to competing orders and exotic quantum phases in frustrated spin systems [22]. In particular, the ability to tune the relative strengths of nearest-neighbor (J1J_{1}), next-nearest-neighbor (J2J_{2}), and third-neighbor (J3J_{3}) interactions, which are highly constrained in real materials, is predicted to enable the exploration of quantum phase transitions among gapped and gapless spin liquids, valence bond solids, and a variety of magnetically ordered states [23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 6, 31, 32]. However, the full control over J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} in spin systems remains challenging due to the difficulty of tuning interaction strengths and ranges while maintaining the necessary levels of coherence and control.

In this work, we develop a systematic framework for engineering long-range interactions in dipolar Rydberg arrays, enabling the realization of the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} Heisenberg model with precise tunability. By using spatially patterned Floquet engineering of the Rydberg level energies and microwave dressing Rydberg states, we map the periodically driven system onto an effective undriven system with renormalized interaction strengths, yielding precise control over the transverse and longitudinal spin-spin interactions in the XXZ model. As a detailed example, we demonstrate how two distinct modulation frequencies can be used to independently control the ratios J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} and J3/J1J_{3}/J_{1} on a kagome lattice. We further generalize this method to a wide range of lattice geometries using graph theory, where site-dependent modulations correspond to graph coloring strategies. To illustrate its universality, we apply this method to all planar Archimedean lattices, achieving flexible tuning of long-range interactions and overcoming the inherent limitations of power-law decaying interactions. This approach opens a pathway to explore tunable frustrated spin systems and exotic quantum phases induced by long-range interactions in Rydberg arrays.

System and spin models.—We begin our discussion with the general spin-1/2 antiferromagnetic J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} Heisenberg model, which is a fundamental model of quantum magnetism. This is described by the Hamiltonian

H=J1​∑⟨m,n⟩𝐒m⋅𝐒n+J2​∑⟨⟨m,n⟩⟩𝐒m⋅𝐒n+J3​∑⟨⟨⟨m,n⟩⟩⟩𝐒m⋅𝐒n,\displaystyle H=J_{1}\hskip-5.69046pt\sum_{\langle m,n\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{m}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{n}+J_{2}\hskip-5.69046pt\sum_{\langle\langle m,n\rangle\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{m}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{n}+J_{3}\hskip-5.69046pt\hskip-5.69046pt\sum_{\langle\langle\langle m,n\rangle\rangle\rangle}\hskip-5.69046pt\mathbf{S}_{m}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{n}, (1)

for J1,J2,J3>0J_{1},J_{2},J_{3}>0, where ⟨m,n⟩\langle m,n\rangle, ⟨⟨m,n⟩⟩\langle\langle m,n\rangle\rangle, and ⟨⟨⟨m,n⟩⟩⟩\langle\langle\langle m,n\rangle\rangle\rangle denote nearest-neighbor (NN), second-nearest-neighbor (2NN), and third-nearest-neighbor (3NN) interactions, respectively. The competition between such interactions introduces geometric frustration and is known to be crucial for the realization of exotic ordered and QSL phases [33, 34].

To realize and manipulate this model, we consider a system of Rydberg atoms arranged on a lattice, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The spin-up and spin-down states are defined by the Rydberg states, with |↓⟩≡|n​S⟩\ket{\downarrow}\equiv\ket{nS} and |↑⟩≡cos⁡θ​|n′​S⟩−sin⁡θ​|n​P⟩\ket{\uparrow}\equiv\cos\theta\ket{n^{\prime}S}-\sin\theta\ket{nP} [35], where |↑⟩\ket{\uparrow} is encoded as one state from the Autler-Townes doublet formed by strongly driving the |n​P⟩↔|n′​S⟩\ket{nP}\leftrightarrow\ket{n^{\prime}S} transition with Rabi frequency Ωmw\Omega_{\textrm{mw}} and detuning DD (θ=arctan⁡(2​Ωmw/D)/2\theta=\arctan(2\Omega_{\text{mw}}/D)/2). Using these ingredients, one can simulate a generalization of the Heisenberg model called the XXZ model, which is given by

Hxxz=∑μ\displaystyle H_{\textsc{xxz}}=\sum_{\mu} ∑(m,n)∈μJμ±​(Sm+​Sn−+Sm−​Sn+)+Jμz​Smz​Snz,\displaystyle\sum_{(m,n)\in\,\mu}J_{\mu}^{\pm}(S_{m}^{+}S_{n}^{-}+S_{m}^{-}S_{n}^{+})+J_{\mu}^{z}S_{m}^{z}S_{n}^{z}\ ,

where μ\mu indicates the NN, 2NN, or 3NN nature of the couplings.

In the spin basis, the strengths of the “flip-flop” (J±J^{\pm}) and Ising (JzJ^{z}) spin-spin interactions in the XXZ model depend on the exchange terms sin2⁡θ⁡⟨n​S,n​P​|V^ddi|​n​P,n​S⟩\sin^{2}\theta\langle nS,nP|\hat{V}_{\text{ddi}}|nP,nS\rangle and sin2⁡θ​cos2⁡θ⁡⟨n​P,n′​S​|V^ddi|​n′​S,n​P⟩\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta\langle nP,n^{\prime}S|\hat{V}_{\text{ddi}}|n^{\prime}S,nP\rangle, respectively, with V^ddi\hat{V}_{\text{ddi}} representing the dipole-dipole interaction operator; see details in the Supplemental Material (SM) [35]. A flexible choice of these matrix elements and microwave-dressed states allows us to globally tune the relative strengths of transverse and longitudinal interaction terms [35, 36, 37] in this dipolar XXZ model. Importantly however, due to the 1/R31/R^{3} power-law decay of the dipolar interactions with distance (RR), the coupling strengths J2J_{2} and J3J_{3} are typically much smaller than J1J_{1} and the interaction ratios are fixed. This limits the ability to explore the full parameter space of the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} Heisenberg model and access the rich, frustration-induced physics facilitated by long-range interactions in the first place.

Floquet engineering.—To implement the flexible control of long-range interactions, we use periodically time-dependent local modulations to engineer an effective Hamiltonian. This approach is analogous to the shaking of optical lattices, which has been used to realize synthetic gauge fields [38, 39, 4, 41, 42] and for band-structure engineering [43, 44, 45]. In Rydberg tweezer arrays, it has previously been used to control many-body dynamics [8] and extend the Rydberg blockade range [46]. As shown in Fig. 1, addressing light (red) is used to locally shift the energy of the spin-down state. This is realized by an AC Stark shift, i.e., by off-resonantly coupling to an intermediate state |p⟩|p\rangle (e.g., the intermediate state of a two-photon ground-Rydberg transition, as in Ref. 3). For a large detuning Δaddr≫Ωaddr\Delta_{\text{addr}}\gg\Omega_{\text{addr}} (such that induced decay [35] can be ignored), the ||↓⟩\downarrow\rangle state experiences an energy shift of δ=Ωaddr2/Δaddr\delta=\Omega_{\text{addr}}^{2}/\Delta_{\text{addr}}. By modulating the Rabi frequency Ωaddr​(t)\Omega_{\text{addr}}(t) using fast acousto- or electro-optics, one creates an effective target Hamiltonian with renormalized interaction strengths.

Specifically, we consider a periodic onsite energy modulation on the Rydberg state |n​S⟩|nS\rangle, as described by

V⁡(t)=∑m,qδq​sin⁡(ωq​t+ϕm​q)​|n​S⟩​⟨n​S|,V(t)=\sum_{m,q}\delta_{q}\sin(\omega_{q}t+\phi_{mq})|nS\rangle\langle nS|, (2)

where mm indexes the lattice sites and qq indexes the modulation frequencies. Here, δq\delta_{q} is the modulation amplitude, ϕm​q\phi_{mq} is the corresponding phase at site mm, and ωq\omega_{q} is the modulation frequency. The time-dependent modulation of the energy difference between state configurations such as |↓⟩m​|↑⟩n\ket{\downarrow}_{m}\ket{\uparrow}_{n} and |↑⟩m​|↓⟩n\ket{\uparrow}_{m}\ket{\downarrow}_{n} leads to a renormalization of the interaction between spins on sites mm and nn, by effectively diluting their exchange coupling via the transfer of weight to the nonresonant components of Floquet-dressed states (in contrast to the typical use of Floquet dressing to activate otherwise nonresonant interaction terms [48, 49, 38]). One can show that the driven system is well-approximated by an effective time-independent Hamiltonian obtained via a unitary transformation [1, 2], with spin-exchange strengths rescaled as

Jm​neff=Jm​n​∏q𝒥0​(2​δqωq​sin⁡(ϕn​q−ϕm​q2)),J_{mn}^{\text{eff}}=J_{mn}\prod_{q}\mathcal{J}_{0}\left(\frac{2\delta_{q}}{\omega_{q}}\sin\left(\frac{\phi_{nq}-\phi_{mq}}{2}\right)\right), (3)

where Jm​nJ_{mn} denotes the original coupling without modulation, 𝒥0\mathcal{J}_{0} is the zeroth-order Bessel function, and ϕm​q−ϕn​q\phi_{mq}-\phi_{nq} represents the phase difference between sites mm and nn for the frequency ωq\omega_{q} (with frequencies set to be incommensurate in the case of multiple frequencies [35]). This enables independent tuning of the transverse spin-spin interaction terms. Such flexible control allows us to explore exotic, otherwise inaccessible quantum phases in many-body systems, including the distinct spin-liquid phases of the kagome spin-1/2 antiferromagnetic XXZ model [26, 25, 27].

Kagome-lattice Heisenberg model.—A paradigmatic platform for highly frustrated quantum magnetism is the kagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet [52, 53]. The phase diagram of this celebrated model—which is also believed to describe certain layered compounds such as herbertsmithite [54, 55]—is remarkably intricate. Even with only NN (J1J_{1}) interactions, the system can host a time-reversal-invariant U(1) Dirac spin liquid (DSL) state [56]. On adding J2J_{2} and J3J_{3} interactions, the phase diagram is known to harbor a second distinct QSL phase, namely a gapped chiral spin liquid (CSL) [24, 29, 6, 57, 26, 25, 28] that spontaneously breaks time-reversal symmetry, in addition to the DSL phase [58]. Here, we illustrate a dual-frequency modulation protocol to engineer J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} spin models on the kagome lattice with independent control over their ratios. As illustrated in Fig. 2, our approach includes two independent periodic modulations:

Process I (frequency ω1\omega_{1}): A site-resolved modulation δ1​sin⁡(ω1​t+ϕm)​|n​S⟩​⟨n​S|\delta_{1}\sin(\omega_{1}t+\phi_{m})|nS\rangle\langle nS| assigns phases ϕm=0\phi_{m}=0, 2​π/32\pi/3, or 4​π/34\pi/3 to lattice sites (orange, gray, and blue in Fig. 2(a), respectively). Interactions on neighboring sites acquire a renormalization factor of 𝒩1=𝒥0​(2​δ1ω1​sin⁡π3)\mathcal{N}_{1}=\mathcal{J}_{0}\left(\frac{2\delta_{1}}{\omega_{1}}\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right), while pairs with the same phase are unaffected. This selectively modifies J1J_{1} and J3J_{3} interactions, leaving J2J_{2} unchanged.

Process II (frequency ω2\omega_{2}): A complementary modulation δ2​sin⁡(ω2​t+ϕn)​|n​S⟩​⟨n​S|\delta_{2}\sin(\omega_{2}t+\phi_{n})|nS\rangle\langle nS| (Fig. 2(b)) assigns different phases to NN and 2NN sites, thus imprinting a factor of 𝒩2=𝒥0​(2​δ2ω2​sin⁡π3)\mathcal{N}_{2}=\mathcal{J}_{0}\left(\frac{2\delta_{2}}{\omega_{2}}\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right) on J1J_{1} and J2J_{2}, while J3J_{3} interactions between sites that share a common phase are unchanged.

The combination of these two processes renormalizes the interaction coefficients as J1eff=J1​𝒩1​𝒩2,J2eff=J2​𝒩2,J3eff=J3​𝒩1,J_{1}^{\text{eff}}=J_{1}\mathcal{N}_{1}\mathcal{N}_{2},J_{2}^{\text{eff}}=J_{2}\mathcal{N}_{2},J_{3}^{\text{eff}}=J_{3}\mathcal{N}_{1}, yielding the tunable ratios:

J2effJ1eff=1𝒩1​J2J1,J3effJ1eff=1𝒩2​J3J1,\frac{J_{2}^{\text{eff}}}{J_{1}^{\text{eff}}}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{N}_{1}}\frac{J_{2}}{J_{1}},\quad\frac{J_{3}^{\text{eff}}}{J_{1}^{\text{eff}}}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{N}_{2}}\frac{J_{3}}{J_{1}}, (4)

where 𝒩1\mathcal{N}_{1} and 𝒩2\mathcal{N}_{2} are independently controlled by adjusting δ1/ω1\delta_{1}/\omega_{1} and δ2/ω2\delta_{2}/\omega_{2}. This enables suppression or enhancement of J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} and J3/J1J_{3}/J_{1} across different parameter regimes as required. In the absence of Floquet driving, the ratio of couplings J1J_{1}:J2J_{2}:J3J_{3} is set by the dipolar interactions to be 11\,: 3−3/2\,3^{-3/2}\,: 2−3≃1\,2^{-3}\simeq 1\,: 0.192\,0.192\,: 0.125\,0.125, which restricts the tunability of the frustration. For instance, in the isotropic Heisenberg model, the CSL phase emerges only for J3≳J2J_{3}\gtrsim J_{2} [57]; even in the XY limit (JμzJ^{z}_{\mu} == 00), the native dipolar system lies very close to the CSL–DSL phase boundary [26]. Our protocol, however, enables access to interaction ratios unattainable in static kagome systems, such as J2/J1∼0.2J_{2}/J_{1}\!\sim\!0.2 and J3/J1∼0.2J_{3}/J_{1}\!\sim\!0.2, which positions us robustly within a stable CSL phase [6, 24, 28]. Besides, unlike materials with immutable spin couplings, this scheme provides in situ control, allowing one to dynamically drive a quantum phase transition from a prepared “simple” phase, such as magnetically ordered states, into regimes with nontrivial topological order [59]. In addition, the system’s inherent longer-range interactions— including two symmetry-inequivalent J3J_{3} and weaker higher-order (e.g., J1eff/J4eff≈18.5J_{1}^{\text{eff}}/J_{4}^{\text{eff}}\approx 18.5) —make the dipolar model distinct from conventional J1J_{1}–J2J_{2}–J3J_{3} models and lead to rich, exotic quantum phases in such frustrated spin systems [31, 7, 8]. While we primarily discuss the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} control, flexible tuning of the distinct J3J_{3} terms [35], along with residual JlJ_{l} terms for l>3l>3, will also be important when considering the precise many-body phases supported under such Floquet control.

Graphically designing spin interactions.— The renormalization mechanism for the kagome lattice suggests a broad and straightforward guiding principle for engineering spin-spin interactions beyond nearest neighbors: (i) identify the two-process color patterns for a given lattice structure; (ii) design the onsite periodic modulation strategy for each color pattern. For step (i), a general method is to map the lattice structure onto a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), where vertices v∈Vv\in V represent lattice sites and edges e∈Ee\in E encode the interaction types (i.e., NN, 2NN, or 3NN). Selectively modulating J1J_{1} and J2J_{2} while keeping J3J_{3} invariant requires vertices connected by third-neighbor edges (em​n∈J3e_{mn}\in J_{3}) to share the same color, while vertices linked by first- or second-neighbor edges (em​n∈J1,J2e_{mn}\in J_{1},J_{2}) adopt distinct colors. This is a graph-coloring problem. The symmetry and connectivity of the graph guide such color filling, enabling us to design the two-process color patterns.

For step (ii), the key principle is to ensure uniform modulation interaction strength for atom pairs separated by the same distance. For lattices with simple color patterns, such as three-color patterns in Fig. 2(a), there are three types of connections (represented by red or black dashed lines), and the renormalization factors for atom pairs are given by Eq. (3). In this case, uniform modulation can be simply achieved using a single frequency, by assigning the phases ϕm=0,2​π/3,4​π/3\phi_{m}=0,2\pi/3,4\pi/3 to the three colors, respectively. However, for more complex colorings (e.g., four-color patterns), a single frequency is insufficient to uniformly modulate all types of links. A systematic solution is to use multifrequency modulation, with details provided in the End Matter and SM [35].

For the most commonly studied lattices—to wit, the kagome, square, triangular, and honeycomb—four-color modulation patterns (or fewer) suffice due to their innate symmetries. This opens the door to accessing a wide variety of correlated many-body phases with Rydberg simulators. For instance, the square-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet hosts Néel-ordered and valence bond solid ground states for varying J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} [62, 63]—with a potential gapless ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL [64, 65] sandwiched between them—while the addition of a nonzero J3/J1J_{3}/J_{1} stabilizes an extended region of the gapless QSL phase [66]. Similarly, the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} triangular-lattice model exhibits a 120∘ Néel-ordered antiferromagnetic ground state and a two-sublattice collinear magnetically ordered state [67], which also competes with a QSL phase [68] that is believed to be a U(1) DSL [69]. With J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} interactions, arguments for both a CSL with spinon Fermi surfaces [70] and a fully symmetric QSL [71] have been proposed. Finally, on the bipartite honeycomb lattice, while various magnetic phases with Néel, valence-bond, and collinear orders have been recognized [72, 73], recent studies have suggested the emergence of a gapless nonmagnetic phase [74] in the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model, as well as QSLs with more complex gauge groups in the easy-axis (Ising) regime [75, 76].

Going beyond these relatively simple lattices, even in geometries requiring up to six-color patterns (with fifteen distinct connections), we show that only four frequencies are needed to achieve uniform modulation for one process [35]. Figure 3 shows the frequency requirements for controlling J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} (one process) and J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} (two processes) interactions across all 11 Archimedean lattices [77, 78] based on the above approach. Besides the four considered earlier, this family of vertex-transitive geometries includes the square-octagon [79], maple-leaf [80, 81, 82, 9, 5], square-hexagonal-dodecagonal (SHD) [85], ruby [86, 87], star [88], trellis [89, 90], and Shastry-Sutherland [91, 92, 93, 94] lattices, which have all been predicted to host a panoply of interesting magnetic phases. Finally, we emphasize that this Floquet renormalization of spin-spin interactions in a geometrically defined manner is broadly applicable, beyond spin-1/21/2 systems [95] and beyond planar lattices [96] and ordered lattices more generally.

Experimental feasibility.—To implement the proposed modulation scheme, the Floquet period should be much shorter than the Rydberg state lifetime. Experimentally, modulation periods ∼\sim 50 ns (frequencies ωq∼\omega_{q}\sim 20 MHz) are readily achievable with acousto-optic devices, well below typical Rydberg lifetimes (1010–100​μ100\,\mus) [97]. The modulation amplitude δq\delta_{q}, set by the AC Stark shift, can be tuned over a broad range—from a few kHz to several tens of MHz—by varying the intensity and detuning of the addressing lasers [3]. This enables δq/ωq\delta_{q}/\omega_{q} to vary continuously from 0 up to order unity, providing wide tunability of the effective interactions [35]. To suppress unwanted tunneling terms, the modulation frequency ω\omega should satisfy Ωmw≫ω≫J\Omega_{\text{mw}}\gg\omega\gg J, where Ωmw\Omega_{\text{mw}} is the microwave driving strength and JJ is the interaction strength. For single-frequency modulation (e.g., when tuning J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} only), this condition is straightforward to meet, as J∼1J\sim 1 MHz is typical in Rydberg systems [98] and Ωmw∼100\Omega_{\text{mw}}\sim 100 MHz is readily achievable in larger bias magnetic fields. For multiple frequency modulation (e.g., in controlling J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3}), the frequency differences |ωi−ωj||\omega_{i}-\omega_{j}| should also obey Ωmw≫|ωi−ωj|≫J\Omega_{\text{mw}}\gg|\omega_{i}-\omega_{j}|\gg J, requiring careful frequency selection but remaining experimentally accessible nonetheless. In this regime of J≈1J\approx 1 MHz, a lattice spacing of about 10 μ\mum and an addressing laser beam waist of roughly 1-2 μ\mum enable precise spatial control with negligible crosstalk to neighboring sites.

In dipolar Rydberg arrays, the required optical modulation patterns can be achieved by simply combining several identical modulated patterns, offset spatially and delayed in their modulation phase. In the complementary platform of dipolar molecule arrays [99, 100, 101], where the scale of exchange interactions is roughly four to six orders of magnitude smaller than in dipolar Rydberg systems, equivalent and even more generic modulation patterns can be achieved simply through direct time-dependent shaping of a single laser field by, e.g., a fast spatial light modulator.

Conclusion.—We present a versatile framework for realizing the most general J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} Heisenberg model in geometrically engineered Rydberg lattices. By leveraging the use of microwave-dressed states [102] and local laser fields to periodically shift the Rydberg energy levels [3], one can realize an effective XXZ or Heisenberg model where transverse spin-exchange terms are precisely engineered, with an effective parameter range beyond that provided by nature. We analyze this approach on the kagome lattice, a geometrically frustrated system, showing how J1J_{1}, J2J_{2}, and J3J_{3} interactions can be independently controlled. Then, we extend the framework to a broad class of lattice geometries using graph theory, mapping lattice structures to graphs with site-dependent modulations determined through graph coloring. Beyond modulating J1J_{1}, J2J_{2}, and J3J_{3}, the approach can be generalized to control spin interactions in more complex scenarios, such as modulating symmetry-inequivalent bonds, as demonstrated in the Supplementary Material (SM) [35].

In the context of utilizing Floquet engineering to access new physics [103], spin systems such as Rydberg arrays stand out as promising platforms. For one, Floquet techniques [104] can be used to engineer new effective Hamiltonian terms [105, 106, 107, 108, 109, 110, 111], without the deleterious higher-band heating effects that plague shaken-lattice experiments [112]. Furthermore, the long-range nature of the interactions even allows for new physics to be accessed by simply changing the relative strengths of existing, competing Hamiltonian terms [113, 114, 46]. Beyond simply reducing the strength of certain interaction terms, Floquet renormalization can also change their sign, which, e.g., could aid the exploration of isotropic dipolar spin interactions in three dimensions. Besides, such tunability may further be used for exploiting long-range interactions in quantum metrology [9, 115, 116, 117] and nonequilibrium physics [118, 119, 120, 121].

End Matter

Appendix A: Multifrequency modulation strategy for complex color patterns.—To achieve uniform modulation strength for atom pairs separated by the same distance, as required in step (ii) above for graphically designing spin interactions, a systematic solution is to apply multifrequency modulation, where each frequency targets a specific subset of connections. This combinatorial approach ensures uniform interaction strengths for all pairs at equal distances.

As a concrete example, we consider the four-color modulation pattern on a honeycomb lattice, illustrated in Fig. 4. The full modulation consists of two processes. Process I is designed to tune the ratio J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} using a two-color pattern, which can be implemented with a single frequency. Modulation at frequency ω1\omega_{1} assigns phases ϕ1′\phi_{1}^{\prime} and ϕ2′\phi_{2}^{\prime} to the blue and orange sites, respectively, as shown in Fig. 4(a). The interactions J1J_{1} and J3J_{3} are renormalized by a factor 𝒩1\mathcal{N}_{1}, given by Eq. (3).

Process II aims to tune J3/J1J_{3}/J_{1} using a four-color pattern, which requires multifrequency modulation. As illustrated in Fig. 4(b), this configuration includes six distinct types of connections between the colored sites. Frequency ω2,A\omega_{2,A} modulates all connections except red–green and yellow–gray; frequency ω2,B\omega_{2,B} excludes red–yellow and green–gray; and frequency ω2,C\omega_{2,C} excludes red–gray and green–yellow. Each connection is modulated by two of the three frequencies. Assuming an identical renormalization factor 𝒩0\mathcal{N}_{0} for each frequency (i.e., δq/ωq=const.\delta_{q}/\omega_{q}=\text{const.}), the combined effective renormalization factor becomes 𝒩02\mathcal{N}_{0}^{2}, applied uniformly across all six connection types. The resulting effective interaction strength is then given by:

𝒩2=𝒥02​(2​δω​sin⁡(ϕ2−ϕ12)),\mathcal{N}_{2}=\mathcal{J}_{0}^{2}\left(\frac{2\delta}{\omega}\sin\left(\frac{\phi_{2}-\phi_{1}}{2}\right)\right), (5)

under the condition ωq/δq≡ω/δ\omega_{q}/\delta_{q}\equiv\omega/\delta. Following this principle, the required modulation frequencies for a given color pattern can be systematically determined. See the SM [35] for a detailed discussion on more complex color patterns.

I Derivation of the effective Hamiltonian

I.1 Mapping to the XXZ model

The dipole-dipole interaction between two Rydberg atoms placed at positions 𝒓m\boldsymbol{r}_{m} and 𝒓n\boldsymbol{r}_{n}, with electric dipole operators 𝒅^m\hat{\boldsymbol{d}}_{m} and 𝒅^n\hat{\boldsymbol{d}}_{n}, is expressed as:

V^ddi=𝒅m^⋅𝐝n^−3​(𝒅m^⋅𝒏)​(𝒅n^⋅𝒏)4​π​ϵ0​R3,\hat{V}_{\mathrm{ddi}}=\frac{\hat{\boldsymbol{d}_{m}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{d}_{n}}-3\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{d}_{m}}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}\right)\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{d}_{n}}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}\right)}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}R^{3}}, (S1)

with R≡|𝒓𝟐−𝒓𝟏|R\equiv\left|\boldsymbol{r}_{\mathbf{2}}-\boldsymbol{r}_{\mathbf{1}}\right| being the distance between the atoms, and 𝒏≡(𝒓𝟐−𝒓𝟏)/R\boldsymbol{n}\equiv\left(\boldsymbol{r}_{\mathbf{2}}-\boldsymbol{r}_{\mathbf{1}}\right)/R the unit vector defining the internuclear axis. Here, we consider dipole-dipole interactions in a perpendicular magnetic field (which sets the quantization axis), where two atoms are placed in the (x,y)(x,y) plane and submitted to a static magnetic field BzB_{z} along the zz direction. The unit vector defining the internuclear axis is 𝒏=(cos⁡ϕ,sin⁡ϕ,0)\boldsymbol{n}=(\cos\phi,\sin\phi,0), with ϕ\phi the angle between the internuclear axis and the xx-axis. In this basis, the dipole-dipole interaction can be written using the components of the dipole operator d^x,d^y\hat{d}^{x},\hat{d}^{y}, and d^z\hat{d}^{z} :

V^ddi=14​π​ϵ0​R3​[d^mz​d^nz+12​(d^m+​d^n−+d^m−​d^n+)−32​(d^m+​d^n+​e−2​i​ϕ+d^m−​d^n−​e2​i​ϕ)]\hat{V}_{\mathrm{ddi}}=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}R^{3}}\left[\hat{d}_{m}^{z}\hat{d}_{n}^{z}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{d}_{m}^{+}\hat{d}_{n}^{-}+\hat{d}_{m}^{-}\hat{d}_{n}^{+}\right)-\frac{3}{2}\left(\hat{d}_{m}^{+}\hat{d}_{n}^{+}e^{-2i\phi}+\hat{d}_{m}^{-}\hat{d}_{n}^{-}e^{2i\phi}\right)\right] (S2)

with d^n±=∓(d^nx±id^ny)/2\hat{d}_{n}^{\pm}=\mp\left(\hat{d}_{n}^{x}\pm i\hat{d}_{n}^{y}\right)/\sqrt{2} for atom nn. These terms can be classified as follows. The first three terms couple states that conserve the total internal angular momentum of the two atoms. Both the d^mz​d^nz\hat{d}_{m}^{z}\hat{d}_{n}^{z} (Δ​mJ=0\Delta m_{J}=0 transitions, with mJm_{J} the projection of the spin angular momentum) terms and the d^m+​d^n−+d^m−​d^n+\hat{d}_{m}^{+}\hat{d}_{n}^{-}+\hat{d}_{m}^{-}\hat{d}_{n}^{+} (Δ​mJ=±1\Delta m_{J}=\pm 1 transitions) terms lead to “flip-flop” interactions where pairs of atoms exchange their internal state, and will be referred to as the spin-exchange terms in the following. The last two terms describe the spin-orbit coupling: those couple two-atom states with different internal angular momenta. The conservation of the total angular momentum requires that these terms carry a phase e±2​i​ϕe^{\pm 2i\phi}. These latter terms—which do not conserve the internal angular momentum—are typically nonresonant in the presence of external fields (due to, e.g., Zeeman shifts), and can generally be ignored except in cases of fine-tuned resonances.

As we now focus on the simple spin-exchange terms of the dipole-dipole interaction, we restrict our analysis to three Rydberg levels labeled as |r1⟩\ket{r_{1}}, |r2⟩\ket{r_{2}}, and |r3⟩\ket{r_{3}}, i.e., |n​S⟩\ket{nS}, |n​P⟩\ket{nP}, and |n′​S⟩\ket{n^{\prime}S} in Fig. 1 of the main text, where nn and n′n^{\prime} are principal quantum numbers. Each level also has a particular set of quantum numbers {J,mJ}\{J,m_{J}\}, with the specific level choices determining the C3C_{3} power-law coefficient of the interactions. The spin-down state is defined as |↓⟩=|r1⟩\ket{\downarrow}=\ket{r_{1}}. The spin-up state is chosen to be a microwave-field-dressed state of an Autler-Townes doublet, split by an energy of ℏ​4​Ωmw2+D2\hbar\sqrt{4\Omega_{\text{mw}}^{2}+D^{2}}, which is generated by strongly driving the |r2⟩↔|r3⟩\ket{r_{2}}\leftrightarrow\ket{r_{3}} transition using a microwave with Rabi frequency Ωmw\Omega_{\text{mw}} and detuning DD. This spin-up state is chosen as one of the two resulting dressed eigenstates: |↑⟩=cos⁡θ​|r3⟩−sin⁡θ​|r2⟩\ket{\uparrow}=\cos\theta\ket{r_{3}}-\sin\theta\ket{r_{2}} for the lower-energy branch or |↑⟩=sin⁡θ​|r3⟩+cos⁡θ​|r2⟩\ket{\uparrow}=\sin\theta\ket{r_{3}}+\cos\theta\ket{r_{2}} for the higher-energy branch, where θ=arctan⁡(2​Ωmw/D)/2\theta=\arctan(2\Omega_{\text{mw}}/D)/2. Physically, these microwave-dressed states of the bare Rydberg levels |r2⟩\ket{r_{2}} and |r3⟩\ket{r_{3}} can be understood as dipoles that oscillate in-phase (lower branch) and out-of-phase (higher branch) with the microwave driving field. Here, without loss of generality, we have implicitly assumed a microwave phase offset of π\pi.

Choosing the lower-energy branch as the spin-up state, the relevant interaction strengths are defined to be Jm​n±=⟨↑⁣↓|​V^ddi​|↓⁣↑⟩m​n=sin2⁡θ​⟨r1,r2|V^ddi|r2,r1⟩m​nJ_{mn}^{\pm}=\bra{\uparrow\downarrow}\hat{V}_{\text{ddi}}\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}_{mn}=\sin^{2}\theta\braket{r_{1},r_{2}|\hat{V}_{\text{ddi}}|r_{2},r_{1}}_{mn} and 4​Jm​nz=⟨↑⁣↑|V^ddi|↑⁣↑⟩m​n=2​sin2⁡θ​cos2⁡θ​⟨r2,r3|V^ddi|r3,r2⟩m​n4J_{mn}^{z}=\braket{\uparrow\uparrow|\hat{V}_{\text{ddi}}|\uparrow\uparrow}_{mn}=2\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta\braket{r_{2},r_{3}|\hat{V}_{\text{ddi}}|r_{3},r_{2}}_{mn}. The parameter θ\theta, which depends on the ratio of the microwave Rabi frequency and the detuning, allows us to globally tune the relative strengths of the transverse and longitudinal interaction terms in this dipolar XXZ model.

With these definitions, the bare Hamiltonian can be written in the spin-1/2 basis as:

H0=\displaystyle H_{0}= ∑m<nJm​n±​(σm+​σn−+σm−​σn+)+4​Jm​nz​(σm0+σmz2)​(σn0+σnz2),\displaystyle\sum_{m<n}J_{mn}^{\pm}\left(\sigma_{m}^{+}\sigma_{n}^{-}+\sigma_{m}^{-}\sigma_{n}^{+}\right)+4J_{mn}^{z}\left(\frac{\sigma_{m}^{0}+\sigma_{m}^{z}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{\sigma_{n}^{0}+\sigma_{n}^{z}}{2}\right), (S3)
=\displaystyle= ∑m<nJm​n±​(σm+​σn−+σm−​σn+)+Jm​nz​σmz​σnz+Jm​nz​(σmz​σn0+σm0​σnz)+Jm​nz​σm0​σn0,\displaystyle\sum_{m<n}J_{mn}^{\pm}\left(\sigma_{m}^{+}\sigma_{n}^{-}+\sigma_{m}^{-}\sigma_{n}^{+}\right)+J_{mn}^{z}\sigma_{m}^{z}\sigma_{n}^{z}+J_{mn}^{z}\left(\sigma_{m}^{z}\sigma_{n}^{0}+\sigma_{m}^{0}\sigma_{n}^{z}\right)+J_{mn}^{z}\sigma_{m}^{0}\sigma_{n}^{0},

where σx,y,z,0\sigma^{x,y,z,0} are the usual Pauli and identity matrices acting on the spin-1/21/2 states |↓⟩\ket{\downarrow} and |↑⟩\ket{\uparrow}, σm+=(σmx+i​σmy)/2\sigma_{m}^{+}=(\sigma_{m}^{x}+i\sigma_{m}^{y})/2, and σm−=(σmx−i​σmy)/2\sigma_{m}^{-}=(\sigma_{m}^{x}-i\sigma_{m}^{y})/2. Up to a constant term ∼σm0​σn0\sim\sigma_{m}^{0}\sigma_{n}^{0}, this is nothing but the Hamiltonian for the XXZ model if one neglects the terms σmz​σn0\sigma_{m}^{z}\sigma_{n}^{0} and σm0​σnz\sigma_{m}^{0}\sigma_{n}^{z}, which may be compensated by single-particle local-field terms near the system boundary. Alternatively, the |↓⟩\ket{\downarrow} state can similarly be formed from a microwave-dressed state to engineer the XXZ model exactly. The Heisenberg point in this model occurs for Jm​n±/2=Jm​nzJ_{mn}^{\pm}/2=J_{mn}^{z}, or equivalently, ⟨↑⁣↓|​V^ddi​|↓⁣↑⟩m​n=⟨↑⁣↑|​V^ddi​|↑⁣↑⟩m​n/2\bra{\uparrow\downarrow}\hat{V}_{\text{ddi}}\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}_{mn}=\bra{\uparrow\uparrow}\hat{V}_{\text{ddi}}\ket{\uparrow\uparrow}_{mn}/2.

In using simple, globally defined dressed states and only applying spatial patterns of temporal modulation to the |n​S⟩\ket{nS} Rydberg level, we show in the following that one can control (through Floquet renormalization) the transverse spin-exchange terms but not the longitudinal Ising-like interactions. Qualitatively, this maps well onto scenarios described by hard-core bosons with tunable dispersion and off-site interactions. While we focus on this experimentally simple situation, we note that added control of the longitudinal spin-spin interactions can be enabled through local and temporal control of the dressing parameter θ\theta.

I.2 Floquet engineering the effective Hamiltonian

We start with the Schrödinger equation with a time-periodic potential V⁡(t)V(t):

i​∂tψ⁡(t)=H⁡(t)​ψ​(t),with​H​(t)=H0+V⁡(t)​and​V​(t+T)=V⁡(t).i\partial_{t}\psi(t)=H(t)\psi(t),\,\text{with}\,\,H(t)=H_{0}+V(t)\,\text{and}\,\,V(t+T)=V(t). (S4)

By considering the unitary transformation ϕ⁡(t)=𝒰⁡(t)​𝝍​(t)=ei​K​(t)​𝝍​(t)\phi(t)=\mathcal{U}(t)\boldsymbol{\psi}(t)=e^{i{K}(t)}\boldsymbol{\psi}(t), the new state ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) satisfies the Schrödinger equation

i​∂tϕ⁡(t)\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\phi(t) =HI​ϕ​(t),\displaystyle=H_{I}\phi(t), (S5)
HI\displaystyle H_{I} =ei​K​(t)​H​(t)​e−i​K​(t)+i⁡(∂ei​K​(t)∂t)​e−i​K​(t),\displaystyle=e^{i{K}(t)}{H}(t)e^{-i{K}(t)}+i\left(\frac{\partial e^{i{K}(t)}}{\partial t}\right)e^{-i{K}(t)},

where we have introduced the interaction Hamiltonian HIH_{I}. Specifically, if one considers K′​(t)=V​(t)K^{\prime}(t)=V(t), the interaction Hamiltonian simplifies to the form of:

HI=𝒰⁡(t)​H0​𝒰†​(t)=ei​K​(t)​H0​e−i​K​(t).H_{I}=\mathcal{U}(t)H_{0}\,\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}(t)=e^{i{K}(t)}{H}_{0}e^{-i{K}(t)}. (S6)

In our case, V⁡(t)V(t) represents the temporal-modulation term, while H0H_{0} corresponds to the dipolar exchange interactions that underlie both the flip-flop and Ising-like terms of the XXZ model. By engineering specific forms of V⁡(t)V(t), we can flexibly tune the dipolar interaction terms. Here, we consider unbiased cases (⟨V⁡(t)⟩=0\langle V(t)\rangle=0), where the renormalized exchange terms are well described as simply being scaled by zeroth-order Bessel functions with tunable modulation indices [1, 2].

Specifically, to achieve flexible control over these interactions in our model, a time-dependent site-specific energy modulation is added solely to the spin-down state (i.e., Rydberg state |r1⟩≡|n​S⟩\ket{r_{1}}\equiv\ket{nS}), with

V⁡(t)=∑m,qδq​sin⁡(ωq​t+ϕm​q)​|↓⟩m​⟨↓|m=∑m,qδq​sin⁡(ωq​t+ϕm​q)​σm−​σm+,V(t)=\sum_{m,q}\delta_{q}\sin(\omega_{q}t+\phi_{mq})\ket{\downarrow}_{m}\bra{\downarrow}_{m}=\sum_{m,q}\delta_{q}\sin(\omega_{q}t+\phi_{mq})\sigma_{m}^{-}\sigma_{m}^{+}, (S7)

where mm indexes the lattice sites and qq represents distinct modulation frequencies. As we describe below, the different frequencies are assumed to be incommensurate so as to treat them as effectively independent modulation processes (ignoring weak higher-order multiphoton processes).

As mentioned in the main text, the local energy shifts δ\delta can be applied as in Ref. 3, through an AC Stark shift induced by off-resonantly coupling to another internal level with focused laser beams. The nominal choice is to couple off-resonantly to the intermediate state (labeled as |p⟩\ket{p} in Fig. 1 of the main text) that also serves as part of a two-photon excitation scheme. In this case, using tightly focused lasers with micron-scale waists can realistically achieve resonant Rabi coupling strengths Ωaddr\Omega_{\textrm{addr}} of up to hundreds of MHz, and one can detune from the |p⟩\ket{p} state on the scale of hundreds to thousands of MHz to ensure an off-resonance condition, Δ≫Ωaddr\Delta\gg\Omega_{\textrm{addr}}. Here, the induced shift will be δ≈Ωaddr2/Δ\delta\approx\Omega_{\textrm{addr}}^{2}/\Delta, on the scale of several tens of MHz. On intermediate timescales and for large detunings, one can ignore Rydberg de-excitations induced by this coupling light, which scale as γind≈Γp​(Ωaddr/Δ)2\gamma_{\textrm{ind}}\approx\Gamma_{p}({\Omega_{\textrm{addr}}}/{\Delta})^{2}, with Γp\Gamma_{p} the decay rate of the intermediate state |p⟩\ket{p} (being roughly 2​π×12\pi\times 1 MHz for rubidium and potassium). For large detunings, this induced decay will remain smaller than the natural decay rate of the Rydberg levels, and thus, is not a major added limitation to the timescales for coherent evolution. However, when working with a fixed number of |↑⟩\ket{\uparrow} excitations, one also has the ability to perform a judicious choice of measurement so as to post-select for cases in which no induced decay of the |↓⟩\ket{\downarrow} atoms has occurred.

By modulating the Rabi frequency Ωaddr​(t)\Omega_{\text{addr}}(t) (via the laser intensity) using fast acousto-optic or electro-optic (amplitude) modulators (AOMs or EOMs), one can generate the desired time-periodic AC Stark shifts, thereby realizing Floquet modulation. Each modulation corresponds to a distinct spatial pattern (color), and the required global optical modulation patterns can be achieved by simply combining several different modulation patterns. As this scheme is based on optical fields, the phase control can be implemented with high spatial and temporal precision, with negligible associated errors. To note, the phase of the modulation is not controlled by the actual phase of the laser fields, but rather by the phase of the laser intensity modulation (with modulation at a frequency ωq\omega_{q}). Here, we note several technical considerations. In one possible implementation, the separate phases ϕm​q\phi_{mq} would be individually controlled via separately driven AOMs or EOMs. These relative phases can be calibrated through the atomic response, and the phase relationships would be quite stable for the expected modulation frequencies (on the few-to-tens of MHz scale), insensitive to incidental changes in the optical path lengths (considering the optical paths being separately fiber-coupled to the experimental setup, for example). The magnitude of the modulation depth, δm​q\delta_{mq}, would be the most likely quantity to suffer from instabilities, as it depends on the overlap with the tweezer-prepared atoms and would likely be subject to some degree of non-common-mode alignment noise or drift. This issue could be mitigated through the use of flat-top Stark-shifting beams, which would allow for the individual addressing of atoms while permitting some tolerance to the exact co-alignment with the tweezers used for loading the atom array.

Having discussed these technical considerations, we now return to the Floquet-engineering scheme based on Eqs. (S5) and (S6), considering a rotating frame with

K(t)=∑m,q−δqωqcos(ωqt+ϕm​q)σm−σm+.K(t)=\sum_{m,q}-\frac{\delta_{q}}{\omega_{q}}\cos(\omega_{q}t+\phi_{mq})\,\sigma_{m}^{-}\sigma_{m}^{+}. (S8)

Then, the interaction Hamiltonian takes the form

HI=\displaystyle H_{I}= e−i∑n′,qδqωqcos(ωqt+ϕn′​q)σn′−σn′+(∑m<nJm​n±(σm+σn−+σm−σn+)+Jm​nzσmzσnz)ei​∑m′,qδqωq​cos⁡(ωq​t+ϕm′​q)​σm′−​σm′+\displaystyle e^{-i\sum_{n^{\prime},q}\frac{\delta_{q}}{\omega_{q}}\cos(\omega_{q}t+\phi_{n^{\prime}q})\sigma_{n^{\prime}}^{-}\sigma_{n^{\prime}}^{+}}\left(\sum_{m<n}J_{mn}^{\pm}\left(\sigma_{m}^{+}\sigma_{n}^{-}+\sigma_{m}^{-}\sigma_{n}^{+}\right)+J_{mn}^{z}\sigma_{m}^{z}\sigma_{n}^{z}\right)e^{i\sum_{m^{\prime},q}\frac{\delta_{q}}{\omega_{q}}\cos(\omega_{q}t+\phi_{m^{\prime}q})\sigma_{m^{\prime}}^{-}\sigma_{m^{\prime}}^{+}} (S9)
=\displaystyle= (∑m<nJm​n±e−i⁡(∑qδqωq​cos⁡(ωq​t+ϕn​q))ei⁡(∑qδqωq​cos⁡(ωq​t+ϕm​q))σm+σn−+h.c.)+Jm​nzσmzσnz,\displaystyle\left(\sum_{m<n}J_{mn}^{\pm}e^{-i\left(\sum_{q}\frac{\delta_{q}}{\omega_{q}}\cos(\omega_{q}t+\phi_{nq})\right)}e^{i\left(\sum_{q}\frac{\delta_{q}}{\omega_{q}}\cos(\omega_{q}t+\phi_{mq})\right)}\sigma_{m}^{+}\sigma_{n}^{-}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)+J_{mn}^{z}\sigma_{m}^{z}\sigma_{n}^{z},

so the transverse spin-spin interactions are renormalized by a factor 𝒩m​n\mathcal{N}_{mn} with

𝒩m​n=exp[i(∑qδqωq(cos(ωqt+ϕm​q)−cos(ωqt+ϕn​q))].\mathcal{N}_{mn}=\exp\left[i\left(\sum_{q}\frac{\delta_{q}}{\omega_{q}}\left(\cos(\omega_{q}t+\phi_{mq})-\cos(\omega_{q}t+\phi_{nq}\right)\right)\right]. (S10)

Using the identity cos⁡A−cos⁡B=−2​sin⁡(A−B2)​sin⁡(A+B2)\cos{A}-\cos{B}=-2\sin(\frac{A-B}{2})\sin({\frac{A+B}{2}}), and the Jacobi-Anger identity

ei​z​sin⁡θ=∑β=−∞∞𝒥β​(z)​ei​β​θ,e^{iz\sin\theta}=\sum_{\beta=-\infty}^{\infty}\mathcal{J}_{\beta}(z)e^{i\beta\theta},

we have

𝒩m​n\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{mn} =exp⁡(i​∑q2​δqωq​sin⁡(ωq​t+ϕm​q+ϕn​q2)​sin⁡(ϕn​q−ϕm​q2))\displaystyle=\exp\left(i\sum_{q}\frac{2\delta_{q}}{\omega_{q}}\sin\left(\omega_{q}t+\frac{\phi_{mq}+\phi_{nq}}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{\phi_{nq}-\phi_{mq}}{2}\right)\right) (S11)
=∏q(∑β𝒥β​(2​δqωq​sin⁡(ϕn​q−ϕm​q2))​ei​β​(ωq​t+ϕm​q+ϕn​q2)).\displaystyle=\prod_{q}\left(\sum_{\beta}\mathcal{J}_{\beta}\left(\frac{2\delta_{q}}{\omega_{q}}\sin(\frac{\phi_{nq}-\phi_{mq}}{2})\right)e^{i\beta\left(\omega_{q}t+\frac{\phi_{mq}+\phi_{nq}}{2}\right)}\right).

Under the conditions that the modulation frequencies are incommensurate and that the rotating-wave approximation (RWA) applies, the higher-order Bessel functions can be neglected, allowing the expression above to be represented by a zeroth-order Bessel function [1, 2, 4], as follows:

𝒩m​n=∏q𝒥0​(2​δqωq​sin⁡(ϕn​q−ϕm​q2)).\mathcal{N}_{mn}=\prod_{q}\mathcal{J}_{0}\left(\frac{2\delta_{q}}{\omega_{q}}\sin\left(\frac{\phi_{nq}-\phi_{mq}}{2}\right)\right). (S12)

This form suggests how the application of time-dependent modulation [Eq. (S12)] provides the means to control the transverse spin-spin interactions. We note that, formally, the use of incommensurate driving frequencies leads to a breakdown of the RWA, as one can always find weak higher-order, multiphoton processes that approximately conserve energy. However, the above form describing renormalized interactions provides a faithful representation on the intermediate timescales relevant to experiments with dipolar Rydberg atoms, which we have confirmed with numerical simulations (see Fig. S4). While Floquet heating would be expected to occur on long timescales (due to the breakdown of the RWA) without mechanisms for entropy removal, such timescales are largely already precluded due to the intrinsic decay of the excited Rydberg levels.

In the next section, we discuss how time-dependent modulation offers great flexibility to engineer the dipolar exchange interactions for various lattice geometries.

II Graphically engineering Hamiltonians for 11 Archimedean lattices

In this section, we present detailed protocols for engineering the spin interactions for the 11 Archimedean lattices. The symmetries and graph properties of the lattices guide us in assigning color patterns, where each color corresponds to a unique local modulation. By choosing appropriate color arrangements, we can systematically control the ratios J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} and J3/J1J_{3}/J_{1}.

Figure S1 shows the color patterns for each lattice. Usually, the first pattern focuses on J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} engineering and can be achieved by coloring all next-nearest-neighbor sites with the same color, while ensuring nearest neighbors differ in color. The second pattern is used for J3/J1J_{3}/J_{1} engineering. In this case, the third-nearest neighbors share the same color, while nearest and next-nearest neighbors each have distinct colors. This strategy works for most Archimedean lattices, with the exception of some special structures; for instance, on the star lattice—due to its triangular-dodecagon structure—achieving identical coloring for all second-order neighbors is not feasible. Instead, we assign different colors to second-order neighbors while ensuring J1J_{1} and J2J_{2} remain distinguishable (a detailed method for handling this case is provided below).

To guarantee uniform modulation of J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3}, it is essential to ensure that connected lattice sites that are the same distance apart experience identical modulation. According to Eq. (S12), for two sites mm and nn with modulations δ​sin⁡(ω​t+ϕm)\delta\sin(\omega t+\phi_{m}) and δ​sin⁡(ω​t+ϕn)\delta\sin(\omega t+\phi_{n}), the effective modulation factor is given by

𝒩m​n=𝒥0​(2​δω​sin⁡(ϕn−ϕm2)).\mathcal{N}_{mn}=\mathcal{J}_{0}\!\left(\frac{2\delta}{\omega}\sin\!\left(\frac{\phi_{n}-\phi_{m}}{2}\right)\right). (S13)

For two-color patterns, simply assigning distinct phases to the two colors is sufficient. For three-color patterns, evenly spacing the phases, such as ϕA=0\phi_{A}=0, ϕB=2​π/3\phi_{B}=2\pi/3, and ϕC=4​π/3\phi_{C}=4\pi/3, ensures uniform modulation between all pairs of colors. For lattices with more color patterns, such as four-color patterns with six distinct connections, a single modulation frequency is not enough. To address this case, we consider multifrequency modulation (as discussed in the End Matter). Each of the frequencies modulates a subset of the connections, ensuring uniform modulation across all connections.

As a detailed example, we show how to modulate the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} spin interactions on a honeycomb lattice by such a multifrequency process in the End Matter of the main text. When considering six-color patterns with up to 15 distinct connections, four frequencies are sufficient to achieve uniform modulation. Figure S2 outlines the phase arrangements and modulation strategies for these cases. Notably, not all four- or six-color patterns demand the maximum number of frequencies. The required frequencies depend on the number of distinct connections involved in interactions with different ranges. For example, in the four-color pattern of the square lattice shown in Fig. S1, J1J_{1} involves only four connections, while J2J_{2} involves two. In this case, two frequencies (ω2,A\omega_{2,A} and ω2,B\omega_{2,B} in Fig. 4 of main text) are sufficient, where J1J_{1} is modulated once and J2J_{2} is modulated twice. Similarly, in six-color patterns, such as those for the star and trellis lattices, two modulation frequencies can achieve uniform modulation across nine connections for J1J_{1} and six for J2J_{2}, as shown in Fig. S3.

Using these principles, we can determine the necessary modulation frequencies and design the corresponding color patterns with the two processes above; the spin interactions are renormalized as: J1eff=J1​𝒩1​𝒩2;J2eff=J2​𝒩2;J3eff=J3​𝒩1.J_{1}^{\text{eff}}=J_{1}\mathcal{N}_{1}\mathcal{N}_{2};\quad J_{2}^{\text{eff}}=J_{2}\mathcal{N}_{2};\quad J_{3}^{\text{eff}}=J_{3}\mathcal{N}_{1}. By independently adjusting (δi,ωi)(\delta_{i},\omega_{i}) in Eq. (S12), one can control 𝒩1\mathcal{N}_{1} and 𝒩2\mathcal{N}_{2} to enhance or suppress specific interactions as shown in Fig. S4. In this example, we focus on the comparatively simple kagome lattice which requires only two-frequency modulation. These simulations confirm that the analytical expressions for the effective renormalized Hamiltonian are in good agreement with the numerical simulations of the system’s dynamics on experimentally relevant timescales. Simulations of lattices requiring five-frequency modulation (not shown) similarly confirm the validity of the expressions for the renormalized interaction on such timescales.

Notably, our approach is not limited to modulating J1J_{1}, J2J_{2}, and J3J_{3} interactions—it can be generalized to control spin interactions in broader scenarios, such as modulation of symmetry-inequivalent bonds with the same distance. As an example, we illustrate the color pattern in Fig. S5 to showcase the control over two types of J3J_{3} interactions on the kagome lattice. Combining with the color pattern in Fig. 2 of the main text, this enables us to control the four symmetry-inequivalent interactions J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3​dJ_{3d}-J3||J_{3||} on the kagome lattice. We note that achieving independent control over the two J3J_{3} interactions motivates the exploration of additional spin models discussed in the condensed-matter literature [6, 7, 8], which may host a wider variety of intriguing quantum phases. Another paradigmatic example is the maple-leaf [Fig. S6(a)], which has three distinct nearest-neighbor (NN) interactions: JdJ_{d} (thick red), JhJ_{h} (blue), and JtJ_{t} (dotted orange). When Jd≫Jt=JhJ_{d}\gg J_{t}=J_{h}, the model exhibits an exact dimer-singlet ground state [5]. This case can be achieved by using a single-frequency Floquet drive with a three-color phase pattern [Fig. S6(b)], with 2​π/32\pi/3 phase difference. Complementarily, alternative color patterns in Figs. S6(c,d) enable different control over the NN interactions. By combining two of the three patterns with two incommensurate frequencies, we can independently tune JdJ_{d}, JhJ_{h}, and JtJ_{t}. This approach offers a way to study the rich phase transitions and exotic physics on the maple-leaf lattice, ranging from magnetic order to disordered phases [9].
